opus-5.5.text:
Validation is a much higher bar than most people realize. In a lot of machine learning applications, being right 95 or even 99 percent of the time is a big win. In driving, the interesting question is what happens in the remaining fraction of a percent, because at the scale of millions of miles those rare cases happen every day.

So I think about it in a few layers.

First, the model has to be good on average, and that's the part the field is comfortable with: benchmarks, held-out data, imitation metrics, and so on. That's necessary but nowhere near sufficient. A planner can look great on average displacement error and still do something unacceptable in a rare interaction, like a cyclist cutting across or a construction zone with a flagger giving ambiguous signals.

Second, you need to understand the long tail. You're not trying to prove the model is perfect. You're trying to build a strong argument that the overall system is safer than a reasonable human baseline, and that it doesn't introduce new kinds of risk humans wouldn't. That means mining for rare scenarios, building scenario libraries, and measuring performance specifically on the hard slices, not just the aggregate.

Third, and I think this is where much of the real work is, you need closed-loop evaluation. Open-loop metrics, where you compare the model's prediction to what a human did in logged data, don't tell you what happens when the car's own decisions change how the world unfolds. So you need simulation that is realistic enough: other agents that react plausibly, sensor simulation where it matters, and a way to run enormous numbers of variations of a situation. A big part of our research has been making simulated agents behave realistically, because if the simulated world is too polite or too strange, your validation results don't transfer.

Fourth, the validation has to be statistically meaningful. When you're talking about events that happen once in hundreds of thousands or millions of miles, you can't just drive and count. You combine real-world driving, structured testing on tracks, large-scale simulation, and targeted adversarial or stress testing, and then you need a principled way to aggregate that evidence into a safety case.

Finally, there's a subtle point about ML models specifically. When you retrain, the model can improve on average but regress in some corner you care about. So validation isn't a one-time gate. It's a continuous process with regression testing on curated hard cases, so every new model is at least as good as the last one wherever safety matters.

To sum up: the standard isn't "the model scores well." It's "we have rigorous, multi-source evidence that the full system behaves safely across the realistic distribution of situations it will face, including the rare ones, and that holds as we keep changing the model." That's a much harder bar, and in many ways it drives our research agenda as much as the modeling itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is that the bar for a self-driving model is fundamentally different from the bar for most machine learning systems, and the difference comes down to what happens in the tail. If you're doing image classification or recommendations, you care about average performance, and a mistake here or there is fine. In driving, the average case is actually not the hard part. Most of the miles are easy. What matters is the rare events, and the standard you need to meet is that the system handles those rare events safely, consistently, and in a way you can actually demonstrate.

So validation for us is not one number. It's a layered thing. At the bottom you have the usual offline metrics on held-out data, which tell you whether the model is improving in aggregate. But that's necessary, not sufficient, because a model can look better on average while regressing on some narrow but critical scenario, like an unprotected left turn with an occluded pedestrian. So on top of that you need targeted evaluation, where you build out collections of scenarios that you care about, including ones you've mined from real driving and ones you've constructed or perturbed in simulation, and you measure behavior on each of them specifically.

Then there's closed-loop evaluation, which I think is really essential and often underappreciated. Open-loop metrics, where you compare the model's prediction to what a human driver did, can be misleading, because small errors compound once the model is actually in control and its own actions change what it sees next. So you have to put the model in a simulator, let it drive, and let the other agents react to it. That's where a lot of the real signal is.

And finally, you need to connect all of that to real-world outcomes. The ultimate standard is something like: is this system safer than a competent human driver, by a meaningful margin, on the roads it's operating on? And you can only make that claim credibly if you've driven real miles, you've looked at the events that occurred, and you've shown that your simulation and your offline metrics actually predict what happens in the real world. If your proxies don't correlate with reality, they're not validation, they're just numbers.

So the short answer is that the standard is high, it's multi-dimensional, and the most important thing is building the machinery that lets you find the problems before they find you.

r003.rationale: It compares the system with a competent human driver on its operating roads, but does not frame the standard in terms of what is reasonable to expect from the vehicle.

astra-6.text:
I think the standard has to be very high, because you’re making decisions that have consequences in the physical world. And it’s not enough to say that, on average, the model performs well. You need to understand where it fails, how you discover those failures, and how the system behaves when it encounters something it hasn’t seen before.

That means validating the whole driving system, not just an individual model on a held-out dataset. A model can improve on a particular metric without necessarily making the vehicle a better driver. You need to connect those measurements to behavior: Does the system anticipate what other road users might do? Does it leave appropriate margins? Can it respond safely when the situation changes?

And you need multiple ways of testing that. Simulation lets you explore scenarios and variations that would be difficult to encounter repeatedly on the road. Controlled testing and real-world driving provide complementary evidence. No single one of those gives you the complete picture.

The particularly challenging part is the long tail. Common situations give you a lot of data, but rare situations can matter enormously for safety. So validation has to be an ongoing process of finding those cases, understanding them, and making sure that when you improve one behavior, you haven’t introduced a problem somewhere else.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the bar has to be very high, because you’re making decisions that have consequences in the physical world. And it’s not enough to show that, on average, the model performs well. You need to understand where it fails, how those failures interact with the rest of the system, and whether you can reliably detect and handle them.

So I think about validation at multiple levels. You evaluate individual components, but ultimately you have to evaluate the driving system as a whole. You need representative driving situations, and you also need challenging, rare situations that you may not encounter very often on the road. Simulation is important there, alongside testing in the real world.

The key question is: what evidence do you have that the system is safe within the conditions where you intend to operate it? A single metric or a certain number of miles isn’t going to answer that by itself.
